executive_summary.narrative: GPT-OSS-120B decode inference on MI355X spends 84.24% of a 2494.24 ms window on compute, with 15.48% GPU idle and communication fully hidden. The MoE expert path dominates end-to-end GPU time (two unfused FP4 expert-GEMM stages at 39.7% of compute), while BF16 GEMMs through the vendor GEMM library are the top roofline-gap bottleneck, running at 30-52% of the matrix compute ceiling. Attention is served by a single fused paged-decode kernel near the HBM roofline. The largest recoverable opportunities are fusing the MoE expert stages and tuning the below-roofline BF16 GEMMs; system-level idle is host-side launch/synchronization bubbles addressable with GPU graph mode.

compute_optimizations.identification:
[P1] Three BF16 matrix multiplies dispatched through the AITER vendor GEMM library were flagged for running below the compute roofline. Two are linear projections inside the transformer graph module (`GptOssForCausalLM` → `OptimizedModule` → `GraphModule`); the third is the logits projection in the language-model head (`ParallelLMHead`). (source: `gemm_metrics.json` → `operations[].efficiency.efficiency_percent` in the 30-60 band, `operations[].efficiency.bound_type` = compute, `operations[].library` = AITER)

[P5] A single BF16 GEMM dispatched through the AITER vendor GEMM library was flagged as memory-bound. It sits in the transformer graph module (`GptOssForCausalLM` → `OptimizedModule` → `GraphModule`) and produces a small N=128 output, consistent with a routing/gate projection. (source: `gemm_metrics.json` → `operations[].efficiency.bound_type` = memory, `operations[].efficiency.efficiency_percent` in the 0-30 band, `operations[].library` = AITER)
compute_optimizations.reasoning:
[P1] The three GEMMs achieve 30.09%, 33.29%, and 52.19% of the 1725 TFLOPS BF16 matrix roofline. Their FLOPS/Byte values (464-522) are far above the compute-bound threshold, confirming the workload is limited by matrix throughput rather than memory bandwidth. The kernels therefore leave a substantial gap between achieved and peak compute.

[P5] The GEMM achieves only 4.94% of the 7.4 TB/s HBM roofline. Its FLOPS/Byte of 102.87 is low, so each byte moved supports little compute reuse and the kernel is bandwidth-limited. The narrow N=128 output dimension gives the matrix engine too little work to hide the weight and activation traffic.
compute_optimizations.resolution:
[P1] Tile-size and wave-occupancy tuning raises the fraction of matrix-engine cycles doing useful MACs, closing the gap to peak. Narrowing precision from BF16 to FP8 raises the matrix roofline from 1725 to 3500 TFLOPS, halving the compute floor for the same shapes when the model tolerates it. Tile size not visible — profile the kernel for tile-size tuning.

[P5] Improving the memory access pattern raises the bytes delivered per unit time, which directly shortens a bandwidth-limited kernel. Because this projection sits alongside its bias-add epilogue in the same parent module, fusing that epilogue eliminates an intermediate write-back and read, cutting bytes moved per invocation — defer that fusion opportunity to the kernel fusion analysis.

compute_optimizations.identification: This operation is the first stage of the GPT-OSS MoE expert path (`GptOssForCausalLM` -> `GraphModule`), launched from the AITER flydsl stage-1 wrapper. It fuses the FC1 GEMM with SiLU and a gating multiply but remains a distinct kernel launch from the FC2 stage, so it is bucketed as unfused. It has no roofline performance model, so it is flagged on its E2E GPU-time share rather than a roofline gap. The backend library is not identified in the trace (source: `moe_unfused_metrics.json` -> `category_findings[0]`, `members[].type` = `unmodeled_significant`, `operations[].library` = null, `operations[].module_chain`).
compute_optimizations.reasoning: This stage carries the largest share of end-to-end GPU time in the whole compute set. It is launched as a separate GEMM from the FC2 stage, so it pays its own kernel-launch overhead and cannot keep the FC1 output on-chip for the downstream FC2. The intermediate activation must be written back to HBM and reloaded by the next stage. The op has no performance model, so no roofline-gap claim is made. TB/s, FLOPS/Byte, and efficiency are uniform-routing approximations.
compute_optimizations.resolution: Fusing the FC1, activation, and FC2 stages into a single expert kernel keeps the intermediate activation in on-chip memory instead of writing it out and reading it back, eliminating that HBM round-trip and removing one kernel launch per token group. This cuts the bytes moved per invocation, which is the mechanism behind the estimated recoverable share. Both stages already run at FP4, the narrowest practical precision, so precision narrowing offers no further reduction.

compute_optimizations.identification: This operation is the second stage of the GPT-OSS MoE expert path (`GptOssForCausalLM` -> `GraphModule`), launched from the AITER flydsl stage-2 wrapper. It runs the FC2 GEMM over FP4 expert weights as a separate launch downstream of the FC1 stage. It has no roofline performance model, so it is flagged on its E2E GPU-time share rather than a roofline gap. The backend library is not identified in the trace (source: `moe_unfused_metrics.json` -> `category_findings[1]`, `members[].type` = `unmodeled_significant`, `operations[].library` = null, `operations[].module_chain`).
compute_optimizations.reasoning: This stage is the second of two separate expert GEMM launches per token group. Because it is not fused with FC1, it must reload the FC1 output from HBM rather than consuming it from on-chip memory, and it pays a second kernel-launch overhead. The op has no performance model, so no roofline-gap claim is made. TB/s, FLOPS/Byte, and efficiency are uniform-routing approximations.
compute_optimizations.resolution: Folding this stage into the same fused expert kernel as FC1 lets it read the FC1 output directly from on-chip memory, removing the HBM reload and the extra launch. That is the mechanism that recovers the estimated share of time this stage costs. The stage already runs at FP4, the narrowest practical precision, so precision narrowing offers no further reduction.

compute_optimizations.identification:
[P4] These operations are the full-attention layer of GPT-OSS decode, served by the AITER paged-attention decode kernel `paged_attention_decode_sliding_window` launched via `aiter::pa_decode_gluon`. The layer uses Grouped Query Attention with 8 query heads per KV head, and the sliding-window parameter is disabled so every query attends over the full paged KV cache. It accounts for 283.601 ms, 11.37% of end-to-end GPU time (source: `inferenceattention_metrics.json` → `operations[].kernel_name`, `operations[].launcher_path`, `operations[].library` (AITER), `operations[].classification.workload_profile.gqa_ratio` = 8, `operations[].perf_params.sliding_window` = -1, `operations[].module_chain` = GptOssForCausalLM).

[P6] These operations are the sliding-window attention layer of GPT-OSS decode, served by the same AITER paged-attention decode kernel `paged_attention_decode_sliding_window` launched via `aiter::pa_decode_gluon`, but with the sliding window set to 128 tokens. The layer uses Grouped Query Attention with 8 query heads per KV head. It accounts for 68.94 ms, 2.76% of end-to-end GPU time (source: `inferenceattention_metrics.json` → `operations[].kernel_name`, `operations[].launcher_path`, `operations[].library` (AITER), `operations[].classification.workload_profile.gqa_ratio` = 8, `operations[].perf_params.sliding_window` = 128, `operations[].module_chain` = GptOssForCausalLM).
compute_optimizations.reasoning:
[P4] The kernel is memory-bound with a low arithmetic intensity of 15.74 FLOPS/byte, so runtime is set by how fast the fp8 paged KV cache can be streamed from HBM. It already achieves 79.59% of the HBM bandwidth roofline, so it is close to the memory ceiling and the remaining gap is small. The recoverable time is therefore bounded to roughly 2% of end-to-end GPU time.

[P6] The kernel is memory-bound with an arithmetic intensity of 14.12 FLOPS/byte. The 128-token sliding window caps each query's KV read to a short window, so each invocation moves little data and runs in about 29.9 µs mean versus 123 µs for the full-attention layer. With such a short effective KV length, fixed per-kernel overhead is a large fraction of runtime, which lowers the achieved fraction of the HBM roofline to 43.34%. Short effective sequences naturally show lower efficiency, so part of this gap is expected rather than a defect.
compute_optimizations.resolution:
[P4] The internal tile size of the fused decode kernel is not visible from the trace — Flash tile size not visible, profile the kernel for tile-size tuning. Improving coalescing of the paged KV-cache block reads reduces the number of bytes wasted per HBM transaction, which is the only lever for a memory-bound kernel. Because the kernel is already near the roofline, expected gains are modest. Kernel occupancy is not observable from the trace — kernel running slower than expected, profile occupancy with hardware counters.

[P6] Packing more decode queries into each kernel wave spreads the fixed per-launch setup cost over more useful work, raising the effective bandwidth for this short-window layer. Improving the memory-access pattern of the paged KV-cache reads reduces bytes wasted per HBM transaction, the primary lever for a memory-bound kernel. The internal tile size is not visible from the trace — Flash tile size not visible, profile the kernel for tile-size tuning. Kernel occupancy is likewise not observable — profile occupancy with hardware counters.

compute_optimizations.identification: This finding flags the vendor-fused AITER kernel `_fused_qk_rope_reshape_and_cache_kernel`, launched from `aiter::unified_attention_with_output_base`. It applies rotary position embeddings to the query and key projections and writes the rotated key/value tensors into the paged KV cache in a single launch. The kernel is a synthetic op with no module chain reported, but its name and call path place it on the attention path of the decoder. It is an AITER backend op (source: `fusedrope_metrics.json` -> `operations[].library` = AITER, `operations[].kernel_name`). Sub-category is heuristic — verify against op semantics before acting on it.
compute_optimizations.reasoning: No analytic performance model covers this fused op, so its efficiency versus roofline cannot be computed from the trace. The op is invoked 4608 times over the run, so per-launch overhead is repeated at high frequency. Its share of E2E GPU time (3.98%) is what drives its rank, not a measured roofline gap.
compute_optimizations.resolution: Profiling with hardware counters would confirm whether the kernel is bound by the KV-cache write bandwidth, which is the expected bottleneck for a reshape-and-cache fusion. Batching the RoPE and cache-write launches upstream reduces the number of kernel launches, so fixed per-launch overhead is amortized across more tokens per invocation. Cross-category fusion potential not assessed here — defer to the kernel fusion analysis.

compute_optimizations.identification: This operation is `aiter::dynamic_per_group_scaled_quant`, an AITER-backed kernel that produces per-group scaled MX FP4 output (bf16 input, fp4 output with an fp8-e8m0 scale tensor). The call chain places it inside the GPT-OSS MoE forward path (`GptOssForCausalLM` to MoE `fused_moe` to `fused_dynamic_mxfp4_quant_moe_sort` to `perx32_mx_quant_hip`), so it quantizes expert activations before the fused MoE GEMM. It was flagged because it is memory-bound and runs far below peak HBM bandwidth. Its sub-category is a heuristic `miscellaneous` label — verify against op semantics before acting on it (source: `groupquant_metrics.json` -> `operations[].efficiency.bound_type`, `operations[].library`, `operations[].classification.sub_category`).
compute_optimizations.reasoning: The kernel is memory-bound with a low arithmetic intensity of 0.51 FLOPS/byte, so its runtime is dominated by moving the bf16 input and writing the packed fp4 output plus per-group fp8 scales. At 12.27% of the 7.4 TB/s HBM roofline, it leaves most of the available bandwidth unused across all 4608 invocations. The per-group quantization reads the activation once and writes two output tensors, so a strided or uncoalesced access over the group layout would keep achieved bandwidth well below peak.
compute_optimizations.resolution: Improving the memory access pattern so reads and writes are coalesced over the per-group layout raises the bytes delivered per unit time, directly shrinking the transfer-dominated runtime. Fusing this quantization into the adjacent MoE quant/GEMM stage eliminates the separate write-back and re-read of the intermediate activation, cutting the bytes moved per invocation. Cross-category fusion potential is not assessed here — defer to the kernel fusion analysis. If it remains below its expected bandwidth band after these changes, profile occupancy with hardware counters.

compute_optimizations.identification: This finding flags `aiter::moe_sorting_opus_fwd`, the AITER token-sort/permutation helper that groups tokens by their assigned expert before the fused MoE expert GEMMs run. It sits in the GPT-OSS-120b MoE layer (`GptOssForCausalLM` → `OptimizedModule` → `GraphModule`), launched from the AITER `fused_moe` → `moe_sorting` path. It is the single largest moe_aux member, and it carries no performance model, so it was surfaced as a heuristic finding by E2E GPU-time share (source: `moe_aux_metrics.json` → `category_findings[0]`, `operations[].library` = AITER, `estimate_method` = heuristic).
compute_optimizations.reasoning: The kernel is an index/scatter sort that permutes 640 tokens across their top-4 expert assignments; it moves routing indices and token metadata rather than performing dense math, so it is memory- and latency-bound by nature. It is launched 4,608 times (once per MoE layer per step), and each launch is small (median ~12.7 µs per op across two sub-phases), so aggregate cost is driven by high invocation count of a small kernel rather than a single large kernel. The trace exposes no FLOPs or bytes-moved for this op, so a roofline efficiency cannot be computed and the slowdown cannot be attributed to a specific compute or bandwidth gap from the trace alone.
compute_optimizations.resolution: Amortizing or fusing the per-layer sort with the neighboring gating-softmax and mxfp4-quant-sort steps would cut the number of small kernel launches, reducing fixed per-launch latency that dominates a sub-15 µs kernel. Tile-size and occupancy tuning of the two-phase sort can raise throughput if the kernel is under-occupied. Cross-category fusion potential not assessed here — defer to the kernel fusion analysis. Because the op has no performance model, profile with hardware counters to confirm occupancy before committing to a kernel rewrite.

compute_optimizations.identification: Two RMSNorm variants launched by the AITER backend were flagged for running below the memory-bandwidth efficiency band expected of simple per-token normalization. `aiter::add_rmsnorm` and `aiter::fused_add_rmsnorm_pad_` are both fused residual-add + RMSNorm kernels operating on `(640, 2880)` bf16 activations. They belong to the RMSNorm layers of the GPT-OSS-120B causal language model (`GptOssForCausalLM`), invoked once per transformer block. (source: `rmsnorm_metrics.json` → `category_findings[0].members[]`, `operations[].library` = AITER, `operations[].module_chain`)
compute_optimizations.reasoning: Both kernels are memory-bound with an arithmetic intensity near 0.6 FLOPS/byte, so runtime is gated by how fast the activations move through HBM. Each achieves only ~2.6 TB/s against the 7.4 TB/s peak, about 35% of roofline. A well-behaved memory-bound elementwise kernel on this hardware typically clears 70% of peak bandwidth, so these kernels leave roughly half of the available bandwidth unused. The gap is in the kernel implementation, not the algorithm — the operations are already fused residual-add variants.
compute_optimizations.resolution: Tuning the kernel's memory access pattern lets each wave move more contiguous bytes per HBM transaction, raising sustained bandwidth toward the level simpler elementwise kernels already reach and cutting the time these kernels spend waiting on memory. Reduction strategy not visible — profile the kernel to identify the variant. The exact configuration limiting occupancy is not observable from the trace; generate a reproducer at the `(640, 2880)` bf16 shape for the kernel team.
